extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, judges, and law students studying U.S. patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for preparing, prosecuting, amending, construing, transferring, and litigating patents — with specific criteria for applications, specifications (description), claims, drawings/models, re-issues, disclaimers, extensions, and repeal. Primarily oriented to U.S. practice and court/Patent Office procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Privilege Created and Defined by Letters-Patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent privilege is created and defined by the grant of letters-patent; the grant confers a monopoly measured and limited by the patent as issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters-patent determine the rights created, and those rights are transferable; interpretation is by courts. The Patent Office issues legal and correct letters-patent pursuant to statute and rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant of Letters-Patent Governed by Statute and Patent Office Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Grant of letters-patent is governed by statute and by rules of the Patent Office; the Commissioner, acting Commissioner, and examiners have defined authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents are illegal unless statutory prerequisites are fulfilled; Patent Office practice and procedure control form and some substantive aspects of issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications Must Conform to Legal Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications must conform to legal requirements; if granted, such conformity is presumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are legal requisites of the application (petition, oath, description, claims, drawings/models, fees). Failure to meet requirements can render grant illegal or subject to challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-Matter of Application Must Be a Patentable Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject-matter of the application must be a patentable invention and must not be an invention already patented in the United States by the same inventor (or claimed in a pending application by the same inventor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules govern joinder of inventions, new uses, improvements, combinations, and whether subject-matter is within statutory classes (arts, machines, manufactures, compositions, designs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification: Its Importance and Twofold Object
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification sets forth the contract between the public and the patentee and has a twofold object (description and claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specification both discloses the invention to satisfy public notice/enablement and defines the monopoly by claims; it is central to validity and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification Divisions: Description and Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification has two divisions: the description (the narrative disclosure) and the claim(s) (the definition of the monopoly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both parts are read together; claims are interpreted with reference to the description, drawings, and other parts of the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description Must Disclose the Attributes of the Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must disclose the attributes of the invention — what it is — and set forth particulars that show the invention's nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure should be sufficiently descriptive to distinguish the invention from prior art and to show what the inventor contends is new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description Must Disclose the Manner of Making the Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must disclose the manner of making the invention so that persons skilled in the art can make it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is enablement: the description should provide enough detail for a skilled person to practice the invention without undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description Must Disclose the Mode of Use of the Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must disclose the mode of use of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relevant, describing how to use the invention is part of the enabling disclosure and may affect claim scope/interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description Confined to Three Points
rubrics_metrics.description: The description should be confined to describing the invention's attributes, manner of making, and mode of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superfluous material or matter outside these points can be problematic; focus on the core enabling content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description Sufficient if Sufficient for Persons Skilled in the Art
rubrics_metrics.description: The description is sufficient if it is sufficient for persons skilled in the art (i.e., enablement standard judged by those skilled in the relevant art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sufficiency is a question of fact and is judged in light of the state of the art at the filing date and other parts of the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description Must Be Correct, Complete, and Intelligible
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must be correct (accurate), complete (contain all necessary details), and intelligible (clear and understandable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguity can be fatal; false suggestions or material inaccuracies may invalidate the patent. Correctness, completeness, and intelligibility are defined and applied in cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description's Sufficiency a Question of Fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the description is sufficient is a question of fact for the tribunal considering the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine the totality (specification, drawings, model, state of the art) to determine sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Claim: Its Objects and General Requisites
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims state the objects and general requisites: they are the life of the patent and the measure of the patent privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims define what the patentee regards as his invention; strict rules govern form and content; claims determine infringement and validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Must Claim a Practically Operative Means and a Concrete Art or Instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim must claim a practically operative means and must claim a concrete art or instrument (not a mere abstraction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims to non-operative or purely theoretical subject matter are improper; claims should define a workable, concrete embodiment or method.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Claim Must Claim a Single and Distinct Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim must claim a single and distinct invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joinder of multiple distinct inventions in one claim or in a single application is restricted; claims must be definite and focused.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Claim Must Indicate the Class of Patentable Inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim must indicate the class (art, machine, manufacture, composition, design) of patentable inventions to which the claimed invention belongs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper classification assists examination and construction; claims must be drafted to reflect the proper statutory category.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Claim Must Precisely Define and Distinguish the Invention from Known Inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim must precisely define the invention and must distinguish it from all known inventions (the prior art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that fail to distinguish over prior art are invalid; precision in claim language is essential for both validity and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Claim Must Set Forth the Invention in its Most Perfect Concrete Form
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim should set forth the invention in its most perfect concrete form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to capture a clear, practicable embodiment and to avoid vague, overly broad or speculative language.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Claim Must Correspond with the Description
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim must correspond with the description (claims should be supported by and consistent with the specification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims inconsistent with the description may be defective; claims are interpreted in light of the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Particular Form Required for a Claim; Technical Phrases Allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: No particular form is required for claims; technical phrases may be used when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While form flexibility exists, strict substance rules apply (definiteness, support, operability). Technical language must be clear to skilled persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Must Not Claim a Mere Function or Mere Effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim must not claim a mere function or a mere effect without claiming means/structure to accomplish it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that only recite results or effects without structural or operative limitation are improper and often invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Must Not Claim a Mere Effect and Must Not Be Alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must not be framed as mere effects, nor be stated in alternative (indefinite, multiple incompatible alternatives) form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatives and functional claiming that obscure boundaries of the invention risk indefiniteness or invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims Must Not Be Unnecessarily Multiplied
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must not be unnecessarily multiplied; avoid excessive, duplicative claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office and courts may penalize or reject over-claiming; claims should be purposeful and economically justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder Rules for Claims (Combinations, Elements, Sub-Combinations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules govern joinder of claims for different inventions, combinations, sub-combinations and elements; combinations are treated specially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim for a combination covers only the precise combination claimed; claims may be joined for combinations and for elements when appropriate under rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims for Specific Classes (Art, Machine, Manufacture, Composition, Design, Improvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are general requisites tailored to claims for an art, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, design, and improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each class has distinctive drafting/interpretation rules (e.g., process claims vs. apparatus claims vs. composition claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings, Models, and Specimens When Required
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings, models, and specimens are required in particular cases and must correspond with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings must be clear and full enough to supply the place of a model when appropriate; specimens may be required for compositions of matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing of Application Commences Proceedings; Application Known by Date and Number
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing of the application commences proceedings to obtain a patent; the application is thereafter known by its filing date and number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing establishes priority in many cases; preservation of secrecy and payment of fees are procedural prerequisites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of Application: Form and Merits; Rejection, Amendment, and Appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination covers objections as to form and merits; rejection must be notified with references; applicant may amend, insist, appeal to Examiners-in-Chief or Commissioner and ultimately to courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two main questions in merits examination; procedure for interviews, motions, appeals, and abandonment are set out; amendments have limits (scope tied to original disclosure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment by Unreasonable Delay and Definition of Last Action/Inaction
rubrics_metrics.description: An application may be abandoned by unreasonable delay (e.g., two years from 'last action' may be unreasonable); 'last action' and 'inaction' are defined; unavoidable delay may be excused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must respond timely to Office actions; explicit rules on abandonment and revival exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference Proceedings to Determine Priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Interference proceedings are instituted to determine priority between rival inventors (only between pending applications or an application and an unexpired patent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict procedural rules govern notices of interference, preliminary statements, testimony, evidence, burden of proof, and judgment of priority; estoppel and consolidation rules apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment of Letters-Patent: Clerical Errors, Disclaimers, and Re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters-patent may be amended to correct clerical errors, by disclaimer (to remove excess), or by re-issue to amend defective language under strict conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clerical errors may be corrected without affecting intervening rights; disclaimers are limited (e.g., to excess arising without fraud); re-issue may not change the nature of the invention or expand claims beyond what the original attempted to describe and claim; re-issue requires inadvertence/ mistake (no fraud) and other procedural conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue Principles: Four Propositions Governing Re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-issue is for amending statement only (not subject-matter), must be confined to the invention attempted in the original patent, must be free from fraud (defects arose by inadvertence/mistake), and, when allowable, may be made in any form necessary to secure the actual invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identity of subject-matter is determined by original specification/drawings/model; re-issued patent supersedes original and requires surrender; procedural steps include oath, specification, filing, examination, and possible interferences/appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of Letters-Patent: General Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: General construction rules: (1) patents are to be liberally construed in favor of the inventor; (2) entire patent construed together as an indivisible instrument; (3) words and phrases interpreted, if possible, in their ordinary sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liberal construction does not authorize departure from patent language or an equivocal/elastic interpretation; the nature of the invention is shown by the state of the art at the date of invention and by other acts/circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction: Special Rules (pioneer patents, re-issued patents, claims for principles/functions/effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Special rules apply to pioneer patents, re-issued patents, claims for combinations, improvements, joint inventions, and claims that attempt to cover principles, functions, or effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms like 'substantially as described' and 'generic' admit nuances; claims for an entirety not divisible and terms admitting degrees require careful treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer of Letters-Patent: Assignments and Licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Patented inventions are property and transferable; property in a patented invention is twofold (the invention and the monopoly). Transfers are either assignments (transfer entire interest) or licenses (lesser interests).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms of transfer depend on subject-matter; an assignment before patent is favored; assignments carry implied warranties of title in many cases; transfers do not necessarily carry extensions unless expressly included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment: Form, By Whom, Effect, and Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments are defined; character determined by subject-matter; form has general requisites; assignments before patent may be effective; assignment transfers only the invention specifically assigned and the monopoly created by American patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single assignment may transfer several patented inventions; assignment does not transfer rights of action for past infringements; existing licenses/powers may be affected depending on terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceedings for Repeal of Letters-Patent (in Interest of Prior Inventors and Public)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three classes interested in repeal: infringers, prior inventors, and the public. Different proceedings exist for repeal in the interest of prior inventors and in the interest of the public (e.g., bills in equity in name of U.S.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeal in public interest rests on principles of sovereignty, not mere legislative acts; fraud, lack of patentable subject-matter, or other serious defects may justify repeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of Letters-Patent: Criteria and Procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensions of patents (special acts or Patent Office jurisdiction historically) require application and proof concerning original patentability, value to the public, sufficiency of inventor's remuneration, and effect on public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must file accounts under oath of receipts/expenditures and show diligence in making the monopoly productive; evidence (disinterested testimony, accounts) required; decision of Commissioner may be final in original jurisdiction cases; extensions may be opposed and involve hearings.
